config.title: System Programming Mastery
config.description: Master OS architectures, multi-process fork execution, thread context switching, synchronization (semaphores, monitors, mutexes), virtual memory, and security bugs.

questions.question:
An essay question asks you to describe the layered view of an Operating System. Which components sit directly above and below the API layer?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: Application User Interface (AUI) and OS Kernel

options.label: B
options.text: Hardware Execution Layer and OS Kernel

options.label: C
options.text: OS Kernel and Application Programs

options.label: D
options.text: Device Drivers and Device Controllers

questions.explanation: The layered OS model stack is: Users (top) -> AUI (Shell/Commands) -> API (Libraries/System Calls) -> OS Kernel -> Hardware. Therefore, the API sits between AUI and the OS Kernel.
questions.hint: Think about where library function calls sit relative to the Shell (AUI) and the low-level Kernel code.
questions.diagram:
graph TD
  U["Users"] --> AUI["AUI (Shell/App User Interface)"]
  AUI --> API["API (System Call Interface)"]
  API --> K["OS Kernel"]
  K --> HW["Hardware Layer"]

questions.question:
To write a code-trace analyzing CPU mode transitions, which event causes the CPU to switch from User Mode (1) to Kernel Mode (0)?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: A hardware interrupt, trap, or system call

options.label: B
options.text: A standard C library function execution

options.label: C
options.text: A user-space variable write instruction

options.label: D
options.text: An instruction cache prefetch operation

questions.explanation: When an interrupt, trap, or system call occurs, the hardware automatically switches the mode bit from 1 (User) to 0 (Kernel) and branches to a kernel vector address.
questions.hint: Look at the transition path from User to Monitor mode in dual-mode operation.
questions.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> UserMode
  UserMode --> KernelMode : Interrupt / Trap / Syscall
  KernelMode --> UserMode : Return to User (Set Mode 1)

questions.question: In a Socratic essay explaining why Monolithic Kernels perform faster than Microkernels, which architectural factor is the most critical?

options.label: A
options.text: Monolithic kernels avoid IPC context switch penalties

options.label: B
options.text: Monolithic kernels use simpler machine code designs

options.label: C
options.text: Monolithic kernels completely disable CPU interrupts

options.label: D
options.text: Monolithic kernels allocate memory only on the stack

questions.explanation: Monolithic kernels run all OS services (scheduling, file system, drivers) in the same address space. Accessing a service is a fast function call, whereas in microkernels it requires IPC context switches.
questions.hint: Think about address spaces: where do drivers and systems run in a Monolithic kernel vs a Microkernel?

questions.question: True or False: In a dual-mode CPU, user applications can directly execute privileged instructions when running in User Mode.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: Privileged instructions can only be executed in Monitor/Kernel Mode (mode bit 0). Attempting to run them in User Mode causes a processor exception/trap.
questions.hint: What is the primary role of the CPU mode bit?

options.label: D

questions.explanation: The internal resource manager view of an OS includes the main managers: Process/CPU scheduler, Memory, Resource/Device, and File managers.
questions.hint: Consider the essential physical computer resources that the OS must allocate to running programs.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the role of the System Programmer user class in system design?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Interacts with systems via graphical GUIs only

options.label: C
options.text: Solves high-level business problems in Python

options.label: D
options.text: Configures office networks and local routers

questions.explanation: System programmers write system software (compilers, loaders, linkers, OS components) to control resources and provide an environment for application programmers.
questions.hint: Look at the classification of system programmers vs application programmers and end-users.

questions.question: When explaining OS design goals, which pair correctly matches a User Goal with a System Goal?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: High memory usage AND manual garbage collection

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.explanation: User goals focus on convenience, speed, reliability, and ease of learning. System goals focus on design simplicity, flexibility, reliability, efficiency, and maintenance.
questions.hint: Consider what the person using the computer wants vs what the OS developer wants.

questions.question:
In a code-trace scenario, a program executes an illegal memory write. What sequence is triggered in a dual-mode system?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: CPU raises a trap -> switches to mode 0 -> calls handler

options.label: B
options.text: Program continues execution -> writes to disk directly

options.label: C
options.text: CPU sets mode bit to 1 -> invokes main function again

options.label: D
options.text: OS halts immediately -> system power is powered off

questions.explanation: An illegal memory write violates page protections. The hardware MMU detects this, triggers a trap (software interrupt), switches the mode bit to 0, and runs the kernel's fault handler (e.g. SIGSEGV).
questions.hint: Think about how the hardware responds to a memory protection fault.
questions.diagram:
graph TD
  P["Process Writes Memory"] --> MMU["MMU Checks Address"]
  MMU -->|Illegal| TRAP["Trigger Trap Exception"]
  TRAP -->|Set Mode 0| KH["Execute Kernel Fault Handler"]
  KH --> TERM["Terminate Process (SIGSEGV)"]

questions.question: True or False: The Operating System acts as a resource allocator to resolve conflicting requests for hardware utilization.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: As a resource allocator, the OS manages CPU, memory, I/O devices, and files, resolving conflicts to ensure efficient and fair execution.
questions.hint: What must the OS do when two processes request the same printer or CPU core?

questions.question:
Explain the benefit of the virtual machine approach to OS architecture.
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: It provides complete protection of system resources

options.label: B
options.text: It speeds up program execution to bare-metal speed

options.label: C
options.text: It eliminates the need for physical CPU scheduling

options.label: D
options.text: It runs all hardware components in the user space

questions.explanation: Virtual machines isolate guest operating systems. An error in one virtual machine does not affect other guests or the host system, providing robust security and protection.
questions.hint: Think about isolation: if one guest OS crashes, what happens to the others?
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  VM1["Guest OS 1 (User App)"] --> HW["Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM)"]
  VM2["Guest OS 2 (User App)"] --> HW
  HW --> PHYS["Physical Hardware Layer"]

questions.question:
Which sequence outlines the steps taken during a standard C system call trace like `read(fd, buf, count)`?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: Push arguments -> trap instruction -> mode 0 -> service routine

options.label: B
options.text: Check cache -> branch to main -> trigger timer -> mode 1

options.label: C
options.text: Allocate heap -> copy buffer -> disable MMU -> branch to stack

options.label: D
options.text: Write registers -> fork process -> return 0 -> loop index

questions.explanation: System calls push arguments onto the stack/registers, execute a trap instruction to switch the CPU mode to 0, lookup the syscall index in the vector table, execute the service routine, and return.
questions.hint: How does user space request services from kernel space safely without direct jumps?
questions.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  UserApp->>Library: read(fd, buf, size)
  Library->>Kernel: Trap Instruction (Switch to Mode 0)
  Kernel->>Kernel: Execute Read Syscall Service
  Kernel-->>Library: Return Result (Switch to Mode 1)
  Library-->>UserApp: Return size / status

questions.question: An essay question asks you to compare System Calls and Library Calls. What is the fundamental difference in execution space?

options.label: A
options.text: System calls execute in kernel mode; library calls execute in user mode

options.label: B
options.text: System calls execute in user mode; library calls execute in kernel mode

options.label: C
options.text: System calls execute on the CPU; library calls execute on hard disks

options.label: D
options.text: System calls are written in Java; library calls are written in Assembly

questions.explanation: Library calls (like `strlen`) run entirely in user mode (user space). System calls (like `write`) must switch the CPU to kernel mode (kernel space) via a trap to execute privileged operations.
questions.hint: Think about where the CPU mode bit switches during execution.

questions.question: True or False: User applications invoke system calls directly by executing jump instructions to arbitrary kernel code addresses.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: User applications cannot jump directly to kernel addresses due to memory protection. They must use a trap instruction, which jumps to a fixed, secure kernel vector address.
questions.hint: Does user mode code have permission to execute jump instructions to kernel memory addresses?

questions.question:
You are writing a C program to perform file copying. Which APIs are system calls rather than standard library calls?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: open(), read(), write(), close()

options.label: B
options.text: fopen(), fread(), fwrite(), fclose()

options.label: C
options.text: printf(), malloc(), free(), exit()

options.label: D
options.text: scanf(), strcat(), strcpy(), strlen()

questions.explanation: The calls `open`, `read`, `write`, and `close` are direct POSIX system calls. The `f`-prefixed functions (`fopen`, `fread`) are standard C library wrappers that buffer data in user space.
questions.hint: Identify the low-level, direct OS interfaces vs the buffered standard library wrappers.
questions.diagram:
graph TD
  App["User App"] -->|Library Call| Lib["fopen() / fread() (C Library)"]
  Lib -->|System Call| Sys["open() / read() (OS Kernel)"]
  App -->|Direct Syscall| Sys

questions.question: Which of the following is a system call category related to process control?

options.label: A
options.text: fork(), execve(), wait(), exit()

options.label: B
options.text: socket(), bindv(), send(), recv()

options.label: C
options.text: chmod(), chown(), link(), unlink()

options.label: D
options.text: shmget(), shmat(), semget(), semop()

questions.explanation: `fork`, `execve`, `wait`, and `exit` are system calls used for process creation, execution, synchronization, and termination.
questions.hint: Think about system calls that create, execute, or wait for active processes.

questions.question: When a system call returns an error, how does it traditionally communicate the error type to a C program?

options.label: A
options.text: Returns -1 and sets the global variable errno

options.label: B
options.text: Triggers a hardware abort and reboots the CPU

options.label: C
options.text: Modifies the program counter to jump to main

options.label: D
options.text: Clears the process heap space and sets registers

questions.explanation: In POSIX/Unix systems, system calls return -1 (or NULL) on failure and store the specific error code in the thread-local global variable `errno`.
questions.hint: How do you inspect what went wrong after a failed `open()` or `read()` call?

questions.question:
In a Socratic essay, a student claims 'System calls are slow.' Which of the following is the best way to explain the source of this latency?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: It is caused by the transition overhead between user and kernel space

options.label: B
options.text: It is caused by the slow transmission speed of virtual memory networks

options.label: C
options.text: It is caused by the CPU waiting for the secondary disk spin cycles

options.label: D
options.text: It is caused by compiler optimization passes stripping syscall code

questions.explanation: System call latency comes from context transitions: saving user registers, switching the CPU mode bit, executing kernel checks, restoring registers, and switching mode back.
questions.hint: Think about the operations performed by the CPU when transitioning across the user-kernel boundary.
questions.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  User->>Kernel: Trap (Save registers, Set mode 0)
  Note over Kernel: Execute Service Routine (Latency)
  Kernel-->>User: Return (Restore registers, Set mode 1)

questions.question: True or False: Operating systems use system calls to enforce security boundary checks on all hardware access requests.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: System calls act as the gatekeeper. Because the kernel executes the system call in mode 0, it can validate user parameters and permissions before performing I/O.
questions.hint: Why does the OS prevent user programs from accessing hardware registers directly?

questions.question:
During a syscall execution, what is the role of the system call table?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: It maps syscall numbers to their corresponding kernel function addresses

options.label: B
options.text: It records the list of active user processes currently running in memory

options.label: C
options.text: It stores temporary file descriptors opened by user-space applications

options.label: D
options.text: It caches recently translated virtual memory page frame addresses

questions.explanation: The system call table is a vector array containing the entry points of all syscall handlers in the kernel. The trap handler uses the syscall number as an index to lookup the function address.
questions.hint: How does the kernel trap handler know which function (e.g. sys_read vs sys_write) to execute?
questions.diagram:
graph LR
  Index["Syscall Number (e.g. 3)"] --> Table["Syscall Table"]
  Table -->|Index 3| Handler["sys_read() Kernel Address"]
  Handler --> Exec["Execute Read Routine"]

questions.question: An essay question asks you to trace a program that calls `sys_write`. Which instruction transitions the CPU to privilege level 0 on an x86-64 machine?

options.label: A
options.text: syscall (or int 0x80) instruction

options.label: B
options.text: jmp kernel_entry instruction

options.label: C
options.text: mov reg, kernel_addr instruction

options.label: D
options.text: push kernel_stack instruction

questions.explanation: On modern x86-64 processors, the `syscall` instruction is used. On older x86 systems, the software interrupt instruction `int 0x80` is executed.
questions.hint: Look for the instruction designed specifically to generate a trap/software interrupt.

questions.question:
An essay exam asks you to compare process and thread memory sharing. Which statement correctly describes the memory layout?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: Threads share code, data, and heap; processes share nothing by default

options.label: B
options.text: Threads share code, stack, and heap; processes share stack by default

options.label: C
options.text: Processes share heap and data; threads share only stack structures

options.label: D
options.text: Processes share stack and code; threads share stack and registers

questions.explanation: Threads within a process share the text (code), data, and heap segments. Each thread must have its own private stack and register state for execution control.
questions.hint: Consider which elements of the address space are shared for joint work vs what is needed to track independent functions.
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Process Address Space
    Shared["Shared: Code / Globals / Heap"]

questions.question:
You are tracing the output of a multi-process C program containing `fork()`. Trace the output of this code snippet:
int x = 5; if (fork() == 0) { x *= 2; } else { x += 3; } printf("%d ", x);

options.label: A
options.text: 10 and 8 (in either order)

options.label: B
options.text: 10 and 10 (in either order)

options.label: C
options.text: 8 and 8 (in either order)

options.label: D
options.text: 16 and 5 (in either order)

questions.explanation: `fork()` duplicates the calling process. The child gets a copy of `x` (initially 5) and receives return value 0, executing `x *= 2` (10). The parent receives the child's PID, executing `x += 3` (8). Both execute independently.
questions.hint: Recall that fork() duplicates memory. Do parent and child share the variable 'x' after fork completes?

questions.question: True or False: A thread has its own independent address space separate from other threads in the same process.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: Threads in the same process share the same address space (heap, data, code). Processes have independent address spaces.
questions.hint: Do threads require IPC calls like pipe or shared memory to communicate with sister threads?

questions.question:
In a system where process creation uses `fork()`, what is the relationship between the parent and child process memory states?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: The child gets a duplicate copy of the parent address space

options.label: B
options.text: The child shares all stack frames directly with the parent

options.label: C
options.text: The parent and child execute on the same stack concurrently

options.label: D
options.text: The child memory changes immediately update parent variables

questions.explanation: When `fork()` executes, the child process receives a duplicate copy of the parent's address space. Modern systems optimize this using copy-on-write (COW).
questions.hint: If the parent modifies a global variable after fork(), does it change in the child?
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  Parent["Parent Address Space (x=5)"]
  Parent -->|fork| Child["Child Address Space (x=5 Copy)"]
  Parent -->|Writes x=8| ParentNew["Parent (x=8)"]
  Child -->|Writes x=10| ChildNew["Child (x=10)"]

questions.question: Which of the following elements is stored inside a Process Control Block (PCB)?

options.label: A
options.text: Process state, program counter, registers, memory pointers

options.label: B
options.text: Web browser history, dynamic user databases, source code

options.label: C
options.text: Local variables, function return values, function arguments

options.label: D
options.text: Compiler optimization flags, network routing tables, socket IP

questions.explanation: The PCB stores the process ID, state, program counter (PC), CPU registers, memory management info (page tables), open file tables, and CPU scheduling info.
questions.hint: What data is required by the OS kernel to stop a process and resume it later from the exact same instruction?

questions.question: When implementing threads, why is a context switch between threads of the same process faster than a context switch between different processes?

options.label: A
options.text: No page table reload or TLB flush is required for thread switching

options.label: B
options.text: Threads do not save CPU registers or program counter states

options.label: C
options.text: Thread context switching is handled entirely by hardware timers

options.label: D
options.text: Threads run in user space without triggering kernel mode interrupts

questions.explanation: Because threads of the same process share the address space, the kernel does not need to reload page table pointers (CR3 register on x86) or flush the TLB cache, saving massive overhead.
questions.hint: Think about what memory mapping resources must change when switching processes vs switching threads.

questions.question:
A code trace contains the execution of the system call `execve()`. What happens to the process address space after `execve` returns successfully?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: The old code, data, heap, and stack are replaced by the new program

options.label: B
options.text: The new program runs in a separate child process context

options.label: C
options.text: The heap is preserved while the stack and text are shared

options.label: D
options.text: The CPU registers are preserved while the instruction cache is freed

questions.explanation: `execve` replaces the calling process's entire address space (code, data, heap, stack) with the executable image of the new program. The process ID (PID) remains the same.
questions.hint: Does execve create a new process or reuse the existing one?
questions.diagram:
graph TD
  P1["Process Address Space (Old Program)"] -->|execve| P2["Process Address Space (New Program loaded)"]

questions.question: True or False: If a process terminates, all of its active threads are terminated automatically.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: Because threads exist within the process environment, terminating the process reclaims its shared address space, destroying all member threads.
questions.hint: Can a thread exist without a parent process?

questions.question:
Explain the term 'orphan process' in Unix-like operating systems.
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: A running process whose parent process has terminated

options.label: B
options.text: A child process that has finished execution but has a PCB

options.label: C
options.text: A process that has no open file descriptors in the table

options.label: D
options.text: A thread that has completed its function execution early

questions.explanation: An orphan process is a process whose parent has terminated. Unix systems resolve this by re-parenting the orphan to the root system process (`init` or systemd, PID 1).
questions.hint: Consider what happens to child processes when their parent is killed.
questions.diagram:
graph TD
  Parent["Parent Process (Killed)"] -->|Orphans| Child["Child Process (PID 102)"]
  Init["Init Process (PID 1)"] -->|Adopts| Child

questions.question: In a Socratic essay analyzing thread states, what state is unique to threads compared to processes in a user-level thread library?

options.label: A
options.text: A thread can be blocked while its parent process is running

options.label: B
options.text: A thread has its own independent disk swap allocation space

options.label: C
options.text: A thread can access privileged CPU instructions directly

options.label: D
options.text: A thread can change its code segment at runtime dynamically

questions.explanation: In a ULT library, the library scheduler manages threads. A thread can be marked 'blocked' by the library, but if the OS scheduler doesn't know, it keeps running the parent process.
questions.hint: Think about what the ULT library knows vs what the OS kernel knows.

questions.question:
An essay exam asks you to map the sequence of events during a context switch from Process A to Process B. What is the correct order?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: Save state A -> select B -> restore state B -> jump to B PC

options.label: B
options.text: Select B -> restore state B -> save state A -> jump to B PC

options.label: C
options.text: Jump to B PC -> save state A -> select B -> restore state B

options.label: D
options.text: Save state A -> jump to B PC -> select B -> restore state B

questions.explanation: The context switch sequence must: 1. Save CPU registers and Program Counter of Process A into PCB A. 2. Select Process B using the scheduler. 3. Restore registers and PC from PCB B. 4. Jump to the restored PC of B.
questions.hint: Why must you save the state of A before selecting B?
questions.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  CPU->>PCB A: Save Registers and Program Counter
  Note over CPU: Scheduler selects Process B
  CPU->>PCB B: Restore Registers and PC
  CPU->>Process B: Resume Execution

questions.question: In a Socratic essay explaining context-switching overhead, why does changing the active page table pointer degrade CPU performance?

options.label: A
options.text: It invalidates the Translation Lookaside Buffer cache entries

options.label: B
options.text: It forces the CPU to reinitialize all hardware interrupt vectors

options.label: C
options.text: It deallocates the process heap space and frees variables

options.label: D
options.text: It runs a compiler optimization check on the active program

questions.explanation: When changing page table registers (like CR3 in x86), the TLB cache becomes invalid. The CPU must perform slow main-memory walks for subsequent memory accesses until the TLB is repopulated.
questions.hint: Think about what the TLB caches and how changing memory mappings affects it.

questions.question: True or False: During a context switch, the CPU remains available to execute user program instructions.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: Context switching is pure OS overhead. During the switch, no user instructions are executed; the CPU is dedicated to saving and restoring kernel states.
questions.hint: Is context-switching considered productive work from the perspective of user applications?

questions.question:
Which of the following events triggers a context switch in a time-sharing system?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: A hardware timer interrupt indicating quantum expiration

options.label: B
options.text: A local variable allocation on a thread stack frame

options.label: C
options.text: A successful cache hit resolving an integer read

options.label: D
options.text: A function call return inside user-space application

questions.explanation: In time-sharing systems, a hardware timer triggers periodic interrupts. The interrupt handler calls the scheduler, which decides whether to context switch the running process due to quantum expiration.
questions.hint: Recall what mechanism prevents a process from hogging the CPU forever in multitasking.
questions.diagram:
graph TD
  Timer["Hardware Timer Interrupt"] --> IH["Interrupt Handler"]
  IH --> Sched["OS Scheduler"]
  Sched -->|Quantum Expired| CS["Trigger Context Switch"]
  Sched -->|Run Again| App["Resume Current Process"]

questions.question: Which registers must be saved in the PCB during a context switch to guarantee execution resumes exactly where it was suspended?

options.label: A
options.text: Program Counter (PC) and CPU Stack Pointer (SP)

options.label: B
options.text: Accumulator (ACC) and instruction cache registers

options.label: C
options.text: Frame buffer address and GPU context registers

options.label: D
options.text: Virtual memory page size and disk swap sectors

questions.explanation: To resume, the CPU needs to know the next instruction address (Program Counter) and the active stack frame context (Stack Pointer), alongside general-purpose registers.
questions.hint: What CPU registers track the current instruction and active stack?

questions.question: How does the dispatcher minimize context switch latency in hardware with multiple register sets?

options.label: A
options.text: It switches the active register set pointer instead of saving data

options.label: B
options.text: It disables virtual memory address translations during execution

options.label: C
options.text: It executes all processes concurrently in the same register file

options.label: D
options.text: It compiles the user program directly to bare-metal hardware registers

questions.explanation: Some architectures have multiple hardware register sets. Instead of saving registers to memory, the dispatcher simply changes a pointer to reference a new register set, reducing switch overhead to near zero.
questions.hint: Think about how hardware design can avoid copying data to and from memory.

questions.question:
What is the difference between a mode switch and a context switch?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: Mode switches change privileges; context switches change active processes

options.label: B
options.text: Mode switches switch memory pages; context switches do not save state

options.label: C
options.text: Context switches change mode bit; mode switches change page tables

options.label: D
options.text: Context switches run in user space; mode switches run in kernel space

questions.explanation: A mode switch transitions the CPU between User (1) and Kernel (0) mode within the same process. A context switch changes the active process running on the CPU, involving state saving and loading.
questions.hint: Does a system call by a process always cause the OS to switch to another process?
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  A["Process A User Mode"] -->|Syscall| B["Process A Kernel Mode (Mode Switch)"]
  B -->|Block / Schedule| C["Process B User Mode (Context Switch)"]

questions.question: True or False: System call entry always triggers a full process context switch.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: System call entry causes a mode switch (User to Kernel). A context switch only occurs if the system call blocks (e.g. waiting for I/O) or is preempted by the scheduler.
questions.hint: If a program writes to a file and the data is cached, does the OS immediately switch to another program?

questions.question:
In context-switching, what is the role of the CPU instruction `iret` (interrupt return) on x86 architectures?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A
options.text: Restores saved flags, CS, and IP registers, switching mode to user

options.label: B
options.text: Saves the program counter and stack pointer to the active PCB

options.label: C
options.text: Allocates a new process stack frame and initializes local arrays

options.label: D
options.text: Flushes the Translation Lookaside Buffer and reloads page tables

questions.explanation: The `iret` instruction atomically pops the instruction pointer (IP), code segment selector (CS), and flags register, transitioning the CPU back to User Mode (privilege level 3) to resume the user program.
questions.hint: Identify the instruction that reverses the effects of a hardware interrupt/trap.
questions.diagram:

questions.question: Trace driver abstraction in C: A driver struct contains: `struct dev { void (*init)(void); int (*write)(char*, int); };`. What is the benefit of using this struct of function pointers?

options.label: A
options.text: It allows swapping physical hardware without changing caller code

options.label: B
options.text: It automatically executes the driver functions in parallel CPU cores

options.label: C
options.text: It stores driver execution stacks directly in the CPU register file

options.label: D
options.text: It bypasses the virtual memory translation page table checks in RAM

questions.explanation: This is a Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL). The application calls `dev->write()`. Swapping the driver struct (e.g. from UART to USB) changes the function pointer targets without modifying the application code.
questions.hint: Think about how operating systems manage diverse hardware (like different network cards) using uniform APIs.

questions.question: True or False: Low coupling makes software easier to maintain because changes to one module have minimal impact on other modules.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: Yes, low coupling isolates changes. Modifying the internal logic of module A does not break module B if they interact through a clean, decoupled interface.
questions.hint: If class A accesses the private fields of class B directly, is coupling high or low?

questions.question:
What is the purpose of a Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) in operating system design?

options.label: B
options.text: Translates virtual page numbers directly to physical frame offsets

options.label: C
options.text: Saves process stack registers to the CPU control file on timers

options.label: D
options.text: Buffers print characters on secondary disk swap space allocations

questions.explanation: A HAL is a layer of software that abstracts hardware board layouts, bus registers, and controllers, providing a uniform API to the upper layers of the kernel.
questions.hint: Think about how a single OS kernel binary can run on different motherboards with different chipsets.
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD

questions.question: Which of the following describes 'information hiding' in software engineering?

options.label: A
options.text: Restricting access to internal module details via public interfaces

options.label: B
options.text: Hiding program source code files from the operating system kernel

options.label: C
options.text: Encrypting memory variables to protect them from format string bugs

options.label: D
options.text: Storing process control blocks on swapped secondary storage disks

questions.explanation: Information hiding isolates design decisions by making module internals private (inaccessible to callers) and exposing only what is necessary through a public interface.
questions.hint: What concept is supported by declaring class variables private and exposing them via public properties?

questions.question: In system programming, how do modular design principles support software safety and testing?

options.label: A
options.text: They allow isolating modules to test them under simulated environments

options.label: B
options.text: They completely eliminate memory stack overflow bugs at compile time

options.label: C
options.text: They force all processes to execute in CPU privilege mode level 0

options.label: D
options.text: They store all data variables inside local register files in the CPU

questions.explanation: Modular design enables unit testing. By isolating a module (like a file system parser) behind an interface, developers can mock dependencies and test it in isolation, finding bugs faster.
questions.hint: Think about the benefit of being able to test a module without running the entire operating system.

questions.question:
How is abstraction represented in layered operating system designs?
[EXAMINE DIAGRAM]

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Each layer has its own virtual memory page table directory in RAM

options.label: D
options.text: Each layer disables hardware interrupts during stack frame changes

questions.explanation: In a layered OS, layer N provides services to layer N+1 using interfaces, while hiding its internal implementation details and the details of all layers below it.
questions.hint: Consider the hierarchy: how do higher layers view lower layers in a layered system?

questions.explanation: High coupling is undesirable. It means components are highly dependent on each other, which means changes to one component will ripple through and break other components.

questions.question:

questions.explanation: By treating devices (keyboards, terminals, disks, network sockets) as files, Unix allows applications to use the same uniform system calls (`open`, `read`, `write`, `close`) to interact with any device.

os-abstract-views.definition: User Mode restricts CPU access using mode bit 1. Kernel Mode allows full control using mode bit 0.
An OS architecture where all core services run directly in a single large kernel address space.

system-calls.definition: A standard programming interface wrapping the low-level kernel trap instructions for applications.
A software-generated exception switching the processor to kernel mode to request OS services.

processes-threads.definition: The memory context allocated to a process, containing text, data, heap, and stack segments.
The return value of fork(), which is 0 for the child process and the child's PID for the parent.

context-switching.definition: The sequence of saving registers of process A to PCB A, selecting B, loading B's registers, and jumping.
The CPU cycle time spent saving and loading process states, page tables, and flushing caches.

process-scheduling.definition: A scheduling policy where a running process retains CPU control until it terminates or blocks voluntarily.
A scheduling policy where the kernel can interrupt running processes to reallocate CPU cores.

time-sharing-multitasking.definition: A physical hardware timer chip generating periodic interrupts to invoke the OS scheduler.
Rapid time-slicing process context switching creating the illusion of concurrent execution.

virtual-memory-addressing.definition: Hardware address translation resolving virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers using page tables.
Translation Lookaside Buffer: a high-speed hardware cache in the MMU storing recent page mappings.

caching.definition: The percentage of memory access requests resolved successfully in cache relative to total memory hits.
L1 is tiny, ultra-fast, core-local cache. L3 is larger, slower, and shared among multiple CPU cores.

spooling.definition: Using disk-based staging directories to prevent fast CPU execution from stalling on slow peripherals.
Buffering holds temporary stream data in RAM. Spooling manages sequential device queues on disk.

user-kernel-threads.definition: The limitation where a user-space thread calling a blocking system call suspends its entire parent process.
Kernel threads allowing concurrent execution of multiple threads from the same process on different CPUs.

process-synchronization.definition: A pure software mutual exclusion solution for two processes using shared flag and turn variables.
The synchronization rule ensuring only processes wanting to enter a critical section can decide who enters next.

shared-memory.definition: Mapping the same physical RAM frame directly to page tables of separate processes for zero-copy IPC.
The requirement for developers to use mutexes/semaphores manually to protect shared memory write states.

race-conditions.definition: Concurrency read-modify-write sequences executed on shared mutable states without proper lock protections.
A data race where interleaved writes cause one process to overwrite and discard another process's update.

deadlocks.definition: The four required conditions for deadlock: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.
A closed loop dependency chain of processes where each waits for a resource held by the next process.

semaphores.definition: Atomic semaphore operations: wait (P) decrements/blocks; signal (V) increments/wakes waiting threads.
Counting semaphores manage multiple resources. Binary semaphores act as locks (values restricted to 0 or 1).

monitors.definition: The monitor queue where threads are suspended when calling wait() on a condition variable.
Automatic mutual exclusion enforced inside monitor methods by the compiler or language runtime.

mutexes-locks.definition: A mutual exclusion lock that can only be unlocked by the exact thread that acquired the lock.
A lock using busy-waiting loops, efficient only for short hold times on multi-processor systems.

buffer-overflows.definition: Writing data past local buffer limits on the stack to overwrite SFP and the function return address.
An unsafe C library function copying characters until finding a null terminator without buffer bounds checks.

format-string-bugs.definition: Exploiting printf calls by passing specifiers like %x to read the stack or %n to write to memory addresses.
Writing printf("%s", input) instead of printf(input) to guarantee input is parsed strictly as a string.

command-injections.definition: Concatenating unsanitized inputs containing shell delimiters into strings executed by system() calls.
Special shell operators like semicolons, pipes, and ampersands used to chain and hijack commands.

modular-design-abstraction.definition: Hardware Abstraction Layer: a kernel module hiding board layout and physical registers behind uniform APIs.
Variables containing function entry addresses, enabling dynamic registration of device drivers.
